```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
options(width = 88)
europeanisation <- readr::read_csv("../data/europeanisation_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
devs <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
inference <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_inference.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bw <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_between_within.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cmeans <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_country_means.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
loo <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_loo.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(estimator == "fe_twoway", left_out != "none")

# the rows of the files that the prose quotes
ref <- curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
bwc <- bw |> datawizard::data_filter(outcome == "mcosmo", predictor == "unemp")
bwg <- bw |> datawizard::data_filter(outcome == "mcosmo", predictor == "growth")
pooled <- devs |> datawizard::data_filter(axis == "estimator", option == "pooled_cl")
two_way <- inference |> datawizard::data_filter(estimator == "fe_twoway")

# shares of the curve below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, by the decisions that the
# prose discusses
sig_by_estimator <- curve |>
  datawizard::data_summary(share = 100 * mean(supports & sig), by = "estimator")
sig_by_predictor <- curve |>
  datawizard::data_summary(share = 100 * mean(supports & sig), by = "predictor")
sig_by_form <- curve |>
  datawizard::data_filter(predictor == "unemp") |>
  datawizard::data_summary(share = 100 * mean(supports & sig), by = "pred_form")

# the share of the variance of unemployment and of the cosmopolitan share that
# lies between the 27 country means
between_share <- datawizard::demean(europeanisation, select = c("unemp", "mcosmo"), by = "cntry") |>
  datawizard::data_summary(unemp = var(unemp_between) / var(unemp),
                           mcosmo = var(mcosmo_between) / var(mcosmo))
```

The country-year panel used in the Europeanisation and the economy case study, comprising the 270 rows on which the reproduction, the specification menu and the curve of the claim are built, receives its econometric treatment in this module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd). The case study takes its claim from a study in which the original author reported that poor national economic performance lowers the positive framing of the European Union [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic], and the case study as a whole is presented in full on the [background page](../background.qmd). The module proceeds from the plainest linear model, through clustered standard errors and the two designs of fixed effects, to random effects and the within–between model. It follows on from [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html), on the AR4DS site, and assumes only what that module covers – reading a CSV, a chain of verbs joined by the pipe, and the idea of a model formula.

Every model presented here is fitted when the page is built, on the committed panel and on the small files of results written from it by the workshop pipeline, so that what you read is what the code produces, and every number can be reproduced from the shipped files. The case-study pipeline, stored in the folder `R/` of the site repository, writes these files of results, whose columns are described in the [codebook of the curve](../data/spec_curve_codebook.md) and the [codebook of the displays](../data/displays_codebook.md).

## 1. The country-year level {#sec-aggregation}

The original author modelled individual survey respondents directly, and the sixteen Eurobarometer waves, once pooled, comprise `r format(sum(europeanisation$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` people interviewed across 27 EU member states between 2004 and 2013, each of whom was asked what the European Union means to them. The core exercise of the workshop relies instead on `europeanisation_cy.csv`, which collapses these respondents into **`r nrow(europeanisation)` country-year rows** – 27 countries observed in each of 10 years – with every framing scale averaged within its cell. For country $c$ in year $t$, the cell value is the mean of its respondents' scores,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \frac{1}{n_{ct}} \sum_{i \,\in\, (c,t)} y_{ict} $$

where $y_{ict}$ is the framing scale of respondent $i$ and $n_{ct}$ the number of respondents in that country-year. Unemployment and GDP growth, being national figures in the first place, are attached directly to each cell. Summing the column `n_cy` of the panel recovers the `r format(sum(europeanisation$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` respondents whose answers were averaged into the `r nrow(europeanisation)` rows, and setting the two numbers side by side – the people who were interviewed and the rows analysed by the models – makes concrete what the aggregation does.

The data are therefore nested at three levels – respondents, country-years and countries – and this module remains at the middle level, which offers two advantages. The first advantage is practical, and it is the reason why the workshop can exist at all, since the raw microdata are licensed by GESIS and cannot be redistributed, whereas the derived country-year averages can be released under an open licence and shipped with the materials. The second is that the country-year is the level at which the predictor varies, as every respondent interviewed in Germany in 2010 shares one German unemployment rate for 2010. All the information contained in the data about how unemployment and EU framing move together thus comes from `r nrow(europeanisation)` pairings at the country-year level, however many individuals were interviewed, and aggregating to that level discards almost none of the variation from which the relationship of interest is identified.

Averaging within a cell removes all the variation between the individuals inside it, leaving nothing in the panel about how framing differs across people of different ages, educations or outlooks. The standard errors no longer reflect `r format(sum(europeanisation$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` respondents but `r nrow(europeanisation)` cells, which is why the models presented below report residual degrees of freedom in the low hundreds rather than in the hundreds of thousands. A relationship among country-year averages also need not hold among individuals. Reading an aggregate association as if it described people is the problem of ecological inference described by @Robinson1950EcologicalCorrelationsBehavior, and the panel cannot answer the question at the level of the individual at all, a limitation whose weight depends on what the analysis sets out to measure.

Although no respondent is interviewed twice, the 270 rows form a balanced panel of countries. Since each Eurobarometer wave draws a new sample, the respondents constitute repeated cross-sections, yet, as @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling [p. 122] notes, "insofar as societies are units of analysis ... in an important sense the data derived from such surveys are in fact panel data, since societies are each observed multiple times".

## 2. The linear model {#sec-ols}

Since every model in this module is a variation on one idea, it is worth meeting the idea first in its plainest form. A **linear model** proposes that the outcome is a straight-line function of a predictor plus noise, and for row $i$ of the panel the model reads

$$ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i $$

and each of its symbols has a plain meaning. $y_i$ is the outcome, here the mean cosmopolitan framing score of a country-year, and $x_i$ is the predictor, its unemployment rate. $\beta_0$, the **intercept**, is the expected outcome when the predictor is zero, while $\beta_1$, the **slope**, is the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit rise in the predictor, the number on which every research question in this case study depends. $\varepsilon_i$ is the **error**, comprising everything else that moves the outcome and assumed to average out to zero. **Ordinary least squares** (OLS) estimates the two $\beta$s by choosing the line that minimises the sum of squared errors,

$$ (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = \underset{\beta_0,\,\beta_1}{\arg\min} \sum_i \left( y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i \right)^2 $$

which is what `lm()` (for 'linear model') computes. The name 'least squares' is meant literally, as illustrated on the workshop panel in @fig-ols-squares.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ols-squares
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "The geometry of 'least squares' on the workshop panel. The side of each red square is the error for one country-year – the vertical gap between the point and the line – so its area is that error squared. OLS chooses the line that makes the summed area of all 270 such squares (six of them drawn here) as small as possible. Both axes are standardised, so the squares are drawn to true proportions."
#| code-fold: true
d_std <- europeanisation |>
  datawizard::data_modify(x = as.numeric(scale(unemp)), y = as.numeric(scale(mcosmo)))
m_std <- lm(y ~ x, data = d_std)
d_std <- d_std |> datawizard::data_modify(fit = fitted(m_std), res = resid(m_std))
show_pts <- d_std |>
  datawizard::data_filter(abs(res) > 0.35, abs(res) < 0.95) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("x") |>
  dplyr::slice(round(seq(1, dplyr::n(), length.out = 6)))
ggplot2::ggplot(d_std, ggplot2::aes(x, y)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "grey70", size = 1.2) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(intercept = coef(m_std)[1], slope = coef(m_std)[2],
                       colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::geom_rect(data = show_pts, inherit.aes = FALSE,
                     ggplot2::aes(xmin = x, xmax = x + abs(res),
                                  ymin = pmin(y, fit), ymax = pmax(y, fit)),
                     fill = "#a10000", alpha = 0.15, colour = "#a10000", linewidth = 0.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(data = show_pts, ggplot2::aes(x = x, xend = x, y = fit, yend = y),
                        colour = "#a10000", linewidth = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = show_pts, colour = "#a10000", size = 1.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::coord_fixed() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "unemployment rate (standardised)",
                y = "mean cosmopolitan framing (standardised)") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Nothing in that geometry is tied to a single predictor, and when the model is given two predictors,

$$ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \varepsilon_i $$

the fitted object is no longer a line but a **plane** floating over the grid of the two predictors. The errors remain the vertical gaps between each point and the fitted surface, OLS still minimises the summed squares of those gaps, and each slope acquires the reading that it retains for the rest of this module, $\beta_1$ being the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit rise in $x_1$ *with* $x_2$ *held fixed*. 'Controlling for' means no more than this movement along the plane parallel to one axis, and on the panel GDP growth is the second predictor that the specification menu can add as an adjustment.

With a third predictor the plane becomes a hyperplane that cannot be drawn, but the algebra of the arg-min never changes, and neither does the reading of a coefficient, each slope being a comparison with everything else in the model held level. The sections that follow remain with a single slope until the adjustment for growth returns with the two designs of fixed effects.

The first argument of `lm()` is a **formula**, written `outcome ~ predictor` and read "outcome as explained by predictor". The panel was read into `europeanisation` at the top of the page with `readr::read_csv("../data/europeanisation_cy.csv")`, the `../` being needed because this page is stored in `companion/`, and fitting the model and reading back its results requires two lines:

```{r}
#| label: first-model
first_model <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation)
summary(first_model)
```

```{r}
#| label: first-model-values
#| include: false
fm <- summary(first_model)$coefficients
```

As this output format recurs, with variations, in every model of the module, it is worth reading slowly once. The `Call` restates the model, and the `Residuals` block summarises the estimated errors $\hat\varepsilon_i = y_i - \hat y_i$, the gaps between each observed value and the fitted line. The `Coefficients` table contains the estimates themselves, with one row for each $\beta$ and four columns for each row:

- **Estimate** is $\hat\beta$ itself. The `unemp` row indicates that a one-point rise in the unemployment rate is associated with a fall of about `r insight::format_value(abs(fm["unemp", "Estimate"]), digits = 4)` in the cosmopolitan-framing score, while the `(Intercept)` row indicates that a hypothetical country-year with no unemployment would be expected to score about `r insight::format_value(fm["(Intercept)", "Estimate"], digits = 2)`.
- **Std. Error** is the standard deviation of the estimate across imagined repeated samples, indicating how precisely the data pin the coefficient down, and it serves as the denominator of the `t` value in the next column.
- **t value** is the estimate divided by its standard error, that is, the number of standard errors by which the estimate lies from zero. Being unit-free, it allows the workshop to place every submitted result on one chart, since whatever the scale of the model, its `t` means the same thing.
- **Pr(>|t|)** is the p-value, the probability of a `t` at least this large in magnitude if the true coefficient were zero. Small values are conventionally read as evidence that the association is not merely noise.

Below the table, the **residual standard error** (`r insight::format_value(sigma(first_model), digits = 3)` here) is the estimate of the spread of $\varepsilon$, on **`r df.residual(first_model)` degrees of freedom**, that is, the `r nrow(europeanisation)` observations minus the two $\beta$s estimated. Degrees of freedom measure how many independent pieces of information remain for estimating uncertainty, a count that becomes relevant repeatedly later in the module. **Multiple R-squared** is the share of the variance in the outcome explained by the line, `r insight::format_value(100 * summary(first_model)$r.squared, digits = 1)`% here and thus essentially nothing, while the **F-statistic** comes from a test of all the predictors at once.

Read as a whole, this first model yields no relationship worth reporting. Its slope is small, its `t` of `r insight::format_value(fm["unemp", "t value"], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` lies well inside the range produced by chance, and its p-value is `r insight::format_value(fm["unemp", "Pr(>|t|)"], digits = 2)`. The value recorded for the analyst C6HJR in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], on exactly these `r nrow(europeanisation)` rows, is a clearly negative t = `r insight::format_value(ref$t, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`, significant at the 5% level under the conventional standard errors used by the analyst, a qualification to which [section 4](#sec-inference) returns. As the data are identical in both fits, the difference lies in the structure of the model, which the rest of the module examines step by step.

The standard errors of OLS assume that the `r nrow(europeanisation)` errors $\varepsilon_i$ are **independent and identically distributed**, and the estimate itself is unbiased only if the error is uncorrelated with the predictor. Both assumptions are strained here, since the `r nrow(europeanisation)` rows are 27 countries observed ten times each, and the ten Danish rows share everything durable about Denmark. Those shared national features form part of $\varepsilon$ and are correlated within each country, and as unemployment levels also differ durably between countries, the same features are correlated with $x$ as well. The next three sections address each consequence in turn, first the standard errors and then the estimate itself.

## 3. Clustered standard errors {#sec-pooled}

Applied to a panel, the simple regression of section 2 has a name of its own, **pooled OLS**, because it pools all country-years into one undifferentiated cloud. Written in the two-index notation of the panel, the same equation makes the pooling visible, with one line serving every $c$ and $t$ and nothing in the model recording that rows share a country:

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

R offers several routes to this fit, and the workshop materials use three of these routes: `lm()` from base R, `feols()` from the fixest package [@BergeEtAl2026FastUserfriendlyEconometrics], and `plm()` from the plm package [@CroissantMillo2023PanelDataEconometrics], the toolkit for panel econometrics used by the analysis recorded in the robustness study. Before any new setting is introduced, a useful habit is to **make different functions agree on the model that you already understand**. When two functions return the same numbers under settings that you can name, you know what each function is doing, and when the defaults of the two functions later diverge, you will know which setting has changed.

```{r}
#| label: pooled-three-ways
#| message: false
m_lm  <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation)
m_fx  <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation, vcov = "iid")
m_plm <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation,
                  index = c("cntry", "year"), model = "pooling")

tibble::tibble(
  fitted_with = c("lm()", "feols()", "plm()"),
  estimate  = c(coef(m_lm)["unemp"], coef(m_fx)["unemp"], coef(m_plm)["unemp"]),
  std_error = c(sqrt(vcov(m_lm)["unemp", "unemp"]),
                sqrt(vcov(m_fx)["unemp", "unemp"]),
                sqrt(vcov(m_plm)["unemp", "unemp"]))
)
```

The three rows are identical to every digit, because they come from one estimator under three names, with `vcov = "iid"` asking fixest for the classical standard errors that `lm()` and `plm(model = "pooling")` report by default. This like-for-like fit serves as the point of comparison, and the next step changes one setting only.

The first repair for the problem of correlated errors retains the estimate and corrects its uncertainty. **Cluster-robust standard errors** replace the classical variance formula with one that permits the errors inside each cluster – here, each country – to be correlated in any pattern,

$$ \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta) \;=\; (X'X)^{-1} \Big( \textstyle\sum_{g=1}^{G} X_g' \hat\varepsilon_g^{\vphantom{\prime}} \hat\varepsilon_g' X_g^{\vphantom{\prime}} \Big) (X'X)^{-1} $$

and the notation is less fearsome than it looks, $X$ being the matrix of predictor values and $G$ the number of clusters, the 27 countries. The formula is a sandwich, whose outer 'bread' terms are the ordinary OLS ingredients while the middle 'meat' sums the residuals within each country in a way that keeps every correlation within a country intact instead of assuming it away. Only the standard error changes in this formula, while $\hat\beta$ remains untouched. In the words of @CameronMiller2015PractitionersGuideClusterrobust [p. 317], whose guide is the standard reference on the subject, in such settings "default standard errors can greatly overstate estimator precision".

```{r}
#| label: pooled-clustered
#| message: false
# fixest: one argument
m_cl <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation, cluster = ~cntry)
fixest::coeftable(m_cl)

# the same repair applied to the lm() fit through the sandwich package
lmtest::coeftest(m_lm, vcov = sandwich::vcovCL(m_lm, cluster = ~cntry, type = "HC1"))
```

The two computations agree once their settings are matched. The default small-sample adjustment in fixest corresponds to `type = "HC1"` in sandwich (and to `vcovHC(..., type = "sss")` in plm), and with `type = "HC0"` the numbers would drift apart in the trailing digits, the kind of discrepancy that the like-for-like habit is meant to explain. In substantive terms, clustering multiplies the standard error by `r insight::format_value(fixest::se(m_cl)[["unemp"]] / fixest::se(m_fx)[["unemp"]], digits = 1)`, and the `t` falls from `r insight::format_value(fixest::tstat(m_fx)[["unemp"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(fixest::tstat(m_cl)[["unemp"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`, because the `r nrow(europeanisation)` rows were never `r nrow(europeanisation)` independent pieces of evidence.

Clustering cannot rescue the estimate, and here the pooled estimate itself is the problem. Because the model absorbs no differences between countries, its slope blends two different comparisons, the first following the movement of framing as unemployment rises over time within a single country, and the second contrasting the framing of countries with high and low unemployment in the cross-section. Between the 27 country means lies `r insight::format_value(100 * between_share$unemp, digits = 1)`% of the variance in unemployment on the panel, as does `r insight::format_value(100 * between_share$mcosmo, digits = 1)`% of the variance in the cosmopolitan share, and the cross-section thus carries much of the weight of a pooled fit. In these data the two comparisons point in opposite directions, with the estimates presented in [section 5](#sec-re) at `r insight::format_value(bwc$b_within, digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` within countries and `r insight::format_value(bwc$b_between, digits = 4, style_positive = "plus")` between countries. The pooled slope of `r insight::format_value(coef(m_lm)[["unemp"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` is a blend of the two, close to zero and attached to neither comparison.

The blend is no peculiarity of a single specification, as becomes apparent when pooled OLS is swapped into each of the `r nrow(curve)` specifications on the curve of the claim, with every other choice left as it was. Pooled OLS then puts `r insight::format_value(pooled$below_zero, digits = 1)`% of the fits below zero, against `r insight::format_value(100 * mean(curve$supports), digits = 1)`% of the specifications on the curve, and the pooled fit and its twin on the curve lie on opposite sides of zero in `r insight::format_value(pooled$sign_changes, digits = 1)`% of the pairs. Only `r insight::format_value(pooled$below_zero_sig, digits = 1)`% of the pooled fits lie below zero with a CR2 p-value under 0.05, the test set out in [section 4](#sec-inference). A pooled fit therefore appears to behave as a different quantity rather than as a noisier version of the slope within countries. Models without fixed effects are also the first kind of nonequivalent model named by @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, and pooled OLS is one of the options for the Estimator decision that the workshop keeps off the curve, as recorded on the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-estimand). While clustering remains the right way to report the uncertainty of a pooled fit, the correction does nothing to the sign, because the sign is a property of the estimate and not of its standard error.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Read `data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz`, keep the positive curve and the pooled fits (`curve == "positive"` and `option == "pooled_cl"`), and count the pairs in which the pooled fit and its twin on the curve fall on opposite sides of zero (`mean(sign(r_ca_dev) != sign(r_ca_twin))`). You should recover the `r insight::format_value(pooled$sign_changes, digits = 1)`% quoted above, straight from the committed file.
:::

## 4. Fixed effects {#sec-fe}

The second repair is directed at the estimate itself. The model recorded for C6HJR in the robustness study, which you reproduce in Task 3, is a constrained one, regressing cosmopolitan framing on the unemployment rate with **country and year fixed effects** and nothing else,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta\, x_{ct} + \alpha_c + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

where $\alpha_c$ is a separate intercept for each country and $\gamma_t$ a separate intercept for each year. The country effects $\alpha_c$ absorb everything time-constant about a country – its language, institutions and size, and its enduring baseline level of EU enthusiasm – and the unemployment slope is thus identified only from how a country changes against itself over time, never from the fact that, say, Denmark and Greece differ. The year effects $\gamma_t$ capture everything common to all countries in a given year, including the shocks across the Union and the shared trajectory of the crisis. Two-way fixed effects therefore compare a country with itself over time, net of whatever moved all of Europe together in a given year.

Mechanically there are two equivalent ways to fit this model, and a comparison of the two shows how the estimator works. The literal way estimates every intercept, placing 26 country dummies and 9 year dummies alongside the slope, and is known as the 'least squares dummy variable' route. The efficient way never estimates the intercepts at all, relying instead on the **within transformation**, which subtracts the mean of each country and the mean of each year from both sides,

$$ \left( \bar{y}_{ct} - \bar{y}_{c\cdot} - \bar{y}_{\cdot t} + \bar{y} \right) \;=\; \beta \left( x_{ct} - \bar{x}_{c\cdot} - \bar{x}_{\cdot t} + \bar{x} \right) + \tilde\varepsilon_{ct} $$

where a dot in place of an index means 'averaged over it'. Demeaning removes $\alpha_c$ and $\gamma_t$ from the equation, and OLS on the transformed data recovers exactly the same $\beta$:

```{r}
#| label: fe-three-ways
m_lsdv   <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + factor(cntry) + factor(year), data = europeanisation)
m_within <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation, index = c("cntry", "year"),
                     effect = "twoways", model = "within")
m_twfe   <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp | cntry + year, data = europeanisation, vcov = "iid")

c(lsdv = coef(m_lsdv)["unemp"], plm = coef(m_within)["unemp"],
  feols = coef(m_twfe)["unemp"])
```

The three functions return one number because all three fit one estimator, and of the three summaries the one printed by fixest is the most informative to read:

```{r}
#| label: fe-summary
summary(m_twfe)
```

The slope of `r insight::format_value(coef(m_twfe)[["unemp"]], digits = 5, style_negative = "minus")` indicates that, within a country, a one-point rise in unemployment is associated with a fall of about `r insight::format_value(abs(coef(m_twfe)[["unemp"]]), digits = 4)` in the mean cosmopolitan-framing score, net of common yearly shocks, with a `t` of `r insight::format_value(fixest::tstat(m_twfe)[["unemp"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` (`r insight::format_p(fixest::pvalue(m_twfe)[["unemp"]], stars = FALSE, digits = 4)`). The two R-squared lines report different quantities, of which only the second bears on the research question. The overall adjusted R-squared of `r insight::format_value(fixest::r2(m_twfe, "ar2"), digits = 2)` mostly measures how much the fixed effects themselves explain, since country identities are highly predictive of framing levels, while the **within R-squared** of `r insight::format_value(fixest::r2(m_twfe, "wr2"), digits = 3)` is the contribution of the slope itself, with movements in unemployment explaining about `r insight::format_value(100 * fixest::r2(m_twfe, "wr2"), digits = 0)`% of the variation within countries.

The value recorded for the analyst C6HJR in the robustness study, **t = `r insight::format_value(ref$t, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`** on `r ref$df` degrees of freedom with N = `r ref$n_cells`, is what this model returns and what the workshop reproduces in Task 3.

A further point about this specification recurs on the specification menu. Once fixed effects are present, grand-mean centring the predictor shifts the intercept but leaves the slope and its `t` untouched, while standardising the predictor rescales the slope without moving its `t`, and neither form can thus move a point on a curve ranked by the partial correlation. This is why the curve contains the raw and the logged forms of unemployment and no centred or standardised twin of either.

### What the fixed effects absorb {#sec-absorb}

A fixed effect absorbs every variable that is constant within its group, whether the variable is measured or not. A country effect absorbs anything that takes one value for each country over the decade, and a year effect anything that takes one value for each year across the 27 countries. The national unemployment rate is neither, as it varies from country to country and from year to year, and both sets of effects thus leave it in the model, using only the part of its variation specific to a country-year. The absorption is made visible by the fixest package when a model is given variables already contained in the effects, here the mean unemployment of each country over the decade and the mean unemployment of the 27 countries in each year:

```{r}
#| label: fe-absorb
#| message: false
absorbed <- europeanisation |>
  dplyr::mutate(unemp_country = mean(unemp), .by = cntry) |>
  dplyr::mutate(unemp_europe = mean(unemp), .by = year)

fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_country + unemp_europe | cntry + year,
              data = absorbed, vcov = "iid")
```

Both added variables are removed because of collinearity, since the information carried by these variables is already contained in the effects, and the slope of unemployment equals the slope above to the last digit. The same reasoning indicates how much of the variation in a predictor is removed by the year effects, namely the share of its variation within countries that is common to all countries in the same year:

```{r}
#| label: fe-year-share
within_country <- datawizard::demean(europeanisation, select = c("unemp", "growth"), by = "cntry")
year_share <- c(
  unemp  = summary(lm(unemp_within ~ factor(year), data = within_country))$r.squared,
  growth = summary(lm(growth_within ~ factor(year), data = within_country))$r.squared
)
round(100 * year_share, 1)
```

The year effects absorb `r insight::format_value(100 * year_share[["unemp"]], digits = 1)`% of the variation in unemployment within countries and `r insight::format_value(100 * year_share[["growth"]], digits = 1)`% of the variation in growth, chiefly through the recession of 2009, which reached every member state in the same year. A random intercept for each country, by contrast, absorbs nothing, because it is a draw from a distribution rather than a parameter for each country. A predictor that is constant within countries thus remains in a model with random intercepts, which is why [section 5](#sec-re) can add the country mean of unemployment to a random-effects model, and why multilevel models can estimate the associations of national characteristics removed by fixed effects. Clustering absorbs nothing either, since it changes only the standard errors, as shown in section 3.

It is because of what fixed effects cannot absorb that the workshop builds a causal graph before choosing a specification. Fixed effects do nothing about **time-varying confounding**: anything that changes within a country over the period and moves both its unemployment and its EU framing – a national political scandal, a programme of austerity specific to the country, a swing in the governing party's stance on Europe – is absorbed by neither set of effects and can bias $\beta$. Nor do fixed effects deal with **feedback**, for if EU framing itself feeds back onto economic outcomes, or if both respond to some third driver that varies over time, the model cannot detect either. The simulations reported by @LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse show how much the remedies proposed for reverse causality in panel data depend on assumptions about its timing, and @Halaby2004PanelModelsSociological [p. 507] opens a review of panel models in sociology with Otis Dudley Duncan's warning that "there is widespread, though not well articulated, opinion that in panel analysis the usual obstacles to inference and estimation are suspended for the benefit of the analyst". The limits of fixed effects in this case study are traced in the [causal-graph module](dags.qmd#sec-growth).

### The two fixed-effects designs {#sec-two-designs}

The design fitted by the analyst KQXUE on the same kind of panel has an intercept for each country and none for each year, and when it is fitted beside the two-way model, it yields a slope larger by more than half:

```{r}
#| label: fe-country
m_country <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp | cntry, data = europeanisation, vcov = "iid")
c(two_way = coef(m_twfe)[["unemp"]], country_only = coef(m_country)[["unemp"]])
```

Without year effects, the comparison of a country with itself retains the changes that every member state underwent in the same year, which on this panel make up `r insight::format_value(100 * year_share[["unemp"]], digits = 0)`% of the variation in unemployment within countries. The two slopes are therefore answers to two questions rather than two estimates of one. The two-way design asks whether framing fell in a country in the years in which its unemployment rose by more than the European movement of that year. The country design asks instead whether framing fell in the years in which unemployment in the country was high, whatever happened elsewhere, which leaves this design open to confounding by any shift in framing across Europe that coincided with the crisis. Both designs offer defensible readings of a claim about how national economic performance shapes framing, and the curve retains both designs as two estimands. The choice between the two designs is also the decision that divides the curve. Of the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlation across the `r nrow(curve)` specifications, `r insight::format_value(forks$share[forks$axis == "estimator"], digits = 1)`% is attributable to the Estimator decision, more than to any other decision, and `r insight::format_value(sig_by_estimator$share[sig_by_estimator$estimator == "fe_country"], digits = 1)`% of the specifications with country effects alone lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r insight::format_value(sig_by_estimator$share[sig_by_estimator$estimator == "fe_twoway"], digits = 1)`% of the two-way ones.

Two further decisions concern the predictor. The claim speaks of "poor economic performances", which the paper measures by unemployment and by GDP growth, and both indicators thus represent the claim on the curve, each with and without the other as an adjustment. Within countries, growth leaves the model less to work with, because `r insight::format_value(100 * year_share[["growth"]], digits = 0)`% of its variation within countries is common to all countries in the same year, and the two-way design removes that common part. On the curve, `r insight::format_value(sig_by_predictor$share[sig_by_predictor$predictor == "growth"], digits = 1)`% of the growth specifications lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r insight::format_value(sig_by_predictor$share[sig_by_predictor$predictor == "unemp"], digits = 1)`% of the unemployment ones. Unemployment also enters in two forms, either raw, so that each percentage point counts the same, or logged, so that a rise from 4% to 8% counts as much as one from 10% to 20%, and the claim does not choose between the two forms. Among the unemployment specifications the two forms give similar shares below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, `r insight::format_value(sig_by_form$share[sig_by_form$pred_form == "raw"], digits = 1)`% for the raw form and `r insight::format_value(sig_by_form$share[sig_by_form$pred_form == "log"], digits = 1)`% for the logged one, while the form, as a main effect, is responsible for `r insight::format_value(forks$share[forks$axis == "pred_form"], digits = 3)`% of the variance. The reasoning behind each of the options available for these decisions is presented on the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-estimand).

### Standard errors with few clusters {#sec-inference}

The standard errors of the two-way model above, like those reported by the analyst, treat the `r nrow(europeanisation)` country-years as `r nrow(europeanisation)` independent pieces of evidence. Taking the residuals of the model country by country, and placing each beside the residual of the same country in the previous year, shows that the country-years are not independent:

```{r}
#| label: fe-serial
resid_lag <- europeanisation |>
  datawizard::data_modify(e = resid(m_twfe)) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("cntry", "year")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(e_before = dplyr::lag(e), .by = cntry)
rho <- cor(resid_lag$e, resid_lag$e_before, use = "complete.obs")
rho
```

The residual of a country in one year correlates with its residual in the year before at `r insight::format_value(rho, digits = 2)`, and a country that framed the EU more positively than the model expects in one year thus tends to do so in the next, ten years of one country carrying less information than ten independent observations would. Clustering by country, as in section 3 for the pooled model, allows any pattern of correlation within a country, and with 27 countries the clustered t is referred to G − 1 = 26 degrees of freedom. A second, less visible problem is that the clustered formula works well when the clusters carry similar amounts of information, whereas once country and year effects are removed, the variation in unemployment that is left, the only variation from which the slope is identified, is concentrated in a few countries. Greece contributes `r insight::format_value(loo$variation_share[loo$left_out == "GR"], digits = 1)`% of this variation, Spain `r insight::format_value(loo$variation_share[loo$left_out == "ES"], digits = 1)`% and Poland `r insight::format_value(loo$variation_share[loo$left_out == "PL"], digits = 1)`%, and with few clusters of such unequal weight even the clustered test overstates the evidence. @CameronMiller2015PractitionersGuideClusterrobust [p. 319] call few clusters "the most difficult complication to deal with", adding that "[t]here is no clear-cut definition of 'few'; depending on the situation, 'few' may range from less than 20 to less than 50 clusters in the balanced case".

The remedy used in the workshop is the **CR2** correction proposed by @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard. The ordinary clustered formula uses the residuals of each country as they emerge from the fit, and when one country contributes much of the variation in the predictor, the fit has already been pulled towards that country, leaving its residuals too small and the standard error with them. CR2 enlarges the residuals of each cluster by the amount by which the cluster has pulled the fit towards itself. The CR2 test is then referred to a t distribution whose degrees of freedom are estimated by the Satterthwaite approximation, in the form developed by @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust for models with fixed effects. These degrees of freedom indicate how many clusters effectively carry the information, being close to G − 1 when the clusters weigh alike and far fewer when a few clusters dominate. @ImbensKolesar2016RobustStandardErrors recommend this combination for few and unequal clusters, because it keeps the share of false rejections close to the 5% promised by the test, and CR2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom is the rule by which every point on the curve of the claim is classed. The literature on few clusters also offers a resampling answer, the wild cluster bootstrap, which flips the residuals of whole countries at random to build the distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis [@MacKinnonWebb2017WildBootstrapInference]. The workshop does not use this bootstrap, because its only implementation in R is no longer maintained. The CR2 test requires a single call to the clubSandwich package, written by Pustejovsky:

```{r}
#| label: fe-cr2
#| message: false
# CR2 errors clustered by country (Bell and McCaffrey 2002) with Satterthwaite
# degrees of freedom (Pustejovsky and Tipton 2018), from clubSandwich
clubSandwich::coef_test(m_lsdv, vcov = "CR2", cluster = europeanisation$cntry, coefs = "unemp",
                        test = "Satterthwaite")
```

The CR2 test requires the dummy-variable fit of the model, because the correction operates on the full design matrix, and it reproduces exactly the p-value stored for the curve, since it is computed in closed form and involves no random draws. @tbl-inference-rules presents the three kinds of inference side by side, for the reproduced specification and for its twin with country effects alone.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-inference-rules
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("One estimate under three kinds of inference. The slope and the partial correlation of the data are the same in every row of a design (r = ", insight::format_value(two_way$r_descriptive[1], digits = 3, style_negative = "minus"), " for the two-way design, ", insight::format_value(inference$r_descriptive[inference$estimator == "fe_country"][1], digits = 3, style_negative = "minus"), " with country effects only). Source: `data/display_inference.csv`.")'
#| code-fold: true
inference |>
  datawizard::data_modify(estimator = factor(estimator, c("fe_twoway", "fe_country"))) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("estimator") |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Design = dplyr::if_else(estimator == "fe_twoway", "Two-way", "Country effects only"),
    Inference = c(conventional = "Conventional",
                  cr1_g1 = "Clustered by country (CR1), G − 1 df",
                  cr2_satterthwaite = "CR2, Satterthwaite df")[inference],
    t = insight::format_value(t, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus"),
    df = dplyr::if_else(df == round(df), insight::format_value(df, digits = 0),
                        insight::format_value(df, digits = 1)),
    p = dplyr::case_when(p < 0.0001 ~ "< 0.0001",
                         p < 0.001 ~ insight::format_value(p, digits = 5),
                         .default = insight::format_value(p, digits = 3)),
    `r from the formula` = insight::format_value(r_formula, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")
  ) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:6, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

Across the three kinds of inference, only the verdict on significance changes. Under conventional errors the reproduced result has p = `r insight::format_value(two_way$p[two_way$inference == "conventional"], digits = 4)`, clustered with the standard adjustment p = `r insight::format_value(two_way$p[two_way$inference == "cr1_g1"], digits = 3)`, and under CR2 p = `r insight::format_value(two_way$p[two_way$inference == "cr2_satterthwaite"], digits = 4)` on `r insight::format_value(two_way$df[two_way$inference == "cr2_satterthwaite"], digits = 1)` degrees of freedom, a figure indicating that the 27 countries carry about as much information as ten would, and the result is thus not significant at the 5% level under the rule by which the curve is classed. The design with country effects alone, by contrast, remains significant under every rule. The conventional errors are retained on this page because they are what the analysts reported and what the reproduction task reproduces, yet no point on the curve is classed by those errors.

The last column of the table conceals a trap for anyone who compares results. The conversion of a test statistic into a partial correlation, $r = t / \sqrt{t^2 + \mathit{df}}$, used in the workshop to place different models on [a common scale](meta-analysis.qmd#sec-onescale), recovers the partial correlation of the data only from the conventional t and the residual degrees of freedom of the fit. When fed the clustered t on 26 degrees of freedom, the conversion returns `r insight::format_value(two_way$r_formula[two_way$inference == "cr1_g1"], digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")` instead of `r insight::format_value(two_way$r_descriptive[1], digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`, a larger number for an unchanged association. The curve therefore places every specification by the descriptive partial correlation of its conventional fit and uses the CR2 test only to determine its class, as the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-conversion) explains in placing the five reanalyses.

## 5. Within and between {#sec-re}

Between the pooled and the fixed-effects extremes lies a third estimator, known in econometrics as random effects and in the multilevel tradition as the random-intercept model.

### Random effects {#sec-random-effects}

**Random effects** retains a country term in the model but, rather than estimating 27 separate intercepts, treats the departures of the countries as draws from a distribution,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ct} + u_c + \varepsilon_{ct}, \qquad u_c \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2) $$

so that instead of 27 numbers the model estimates a single one, the variance of the country effects $\sigma_u^2$. Estimation is by generalised least squares, whose mechanics place the estimator on the line running from pooled OLS to fixed effects. Where fixed effects subtract the *entire* mean of each country, random effects subtract a *fraction* $\theta$ of it,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} - \theta \bar{y}_{c\cdot} = \beta_0 (1 - \theta) + \beta_1 \left( x_{ct} - \theta \bar{x}_{c\cdot} \right) + \text{error}, \qquad \theta = 1 - \sqrt{ \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2 + T \sigma_u^2} } $$

with $T$ the number of years for each country. At $\theta = 0$ the estimator is pooled OLS and at $\theta = 1$ it is fixed effects, while the data place it in between according to how much of the total variance lies between countries.

```{r}
#| label: re-fit
m_re <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation,
                 index = c("cntry", "year"), model = "random")
summary(m_re)
```

```{r}
#| label: re-values
#| include: false
re_comp <- plm::ercomp(m_re)
```

The new element in this output is the `Effects` block, in which the **individual** variance (`r insight::format_value(re_comp$sigma2[["id"]], digits = 4)`) is $\hat\sigma_u^2$, the component between countries, and the **idiosyncratic** variance (`r insight::format_value(re_comp$sigma2[["idios"]], digits = 4)`) is $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2$, the noise within countries. The `share` column places `r insight::format_value(100 * re_comp$sigma2[["id"]] / sum(re_comp$sigma2), digits = 0)`% of the error variance between countries. The reported $\theta$ of `r insight::format_value(re_comp$theta[["id"]], digits = 2)` places this fit `r insight::format_value(100 * re_comp$theta[["id"]], digits = 0)`% of the way from pooled OLS towards fixed effects, and the slope duly falls close to the estimate with country fixed effects, at `r insight::format_value(coef(m_re)[["unemp"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` (z = `r insight::format_value(coef(summary(m_re))["unemp", "z-value"], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`) against the `r insight::format_value(coef(m_country)[["unemp"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` given by country fixed effects alone. As the default random-effects model in plm has country effects only, its natural comparator is the one-way design of fixed effects rather than the two-way one.

Random effects is more efficient than fixed effects when its central assumption holds, namely that the country effects $u_c$ are **uncorrelated with the predictor**. In econometrics that assumption has become the very meaning of the term, as @Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross [p. 286] writes: "In modern econometric parlance, a random effects framework is synonymous with zero correlation between the observed explanatory variables and the unobserved effect". In this case the assumption is a strong one, since a country's unemployment level is very likely bound up with the same durable national features that shape its baseline EU framing, which is precisely the correlation that fixed effects were designed to remove. The **Hausman test** [@Hausman1978SpecificationTestsEconometrics] formalises this comparison on the grounds that, if the assumption held, fixed and random effects would estimate the same quantity and differ only by noise, a large gap between the two estimates thus counting as evidence against the assumption. Comparing the two one-way (country) estimators gives

```{r}
#| label: re-hausman
fe_country <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation, index = c("cntry", "year"),
                       effect = "individual", model = "within")
re_country <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = europeanisation, index = c("cntry", "year"),
                       effect = "individual", model = "random")
hausman <- plm::phtest(fe_country, re_country)
hausman
```

and the test rejects (`r insight::format_p(hausman$p.value, stars = FALSE, digits = 4)`), indicating that the estimators disagree by more than chance allows and that the assumption of random effects is hard to defend here. The test, however, rests on an assumption of its own, as its traditional form treats the random-effects estimator as efficient, which requires the errors of a country to be uncorrelated from year to year. That assumption is ruled out by the residual correlation of `r insight::format_value(rho, digits = 2)` reported in section 4, and Wooldridge (p. 333) notes that without it, reading the traditional statistic against its chi-squared distribution "will result in a test that will be undersized or oversized ... and we cannot generally tell which is the case". The within–between model presented below gives the same comparison a form that can be tested under the CR2 rule of the workshop.

### The within–between model {#sec-within-between}

A response arguably more informative than picking a winner is to split the predictor into its two kinds of variation – the *average* unemployment of each country across the decade, and the *departure* of each year from that average – and to give each its own slope. @Mundlak1978PoolingTimeSeries presented the device in its first form, which adds the country mean of the predictor to the random-effects model while leaving the predictor as it is,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta\, x_{ct} + \pi\, \bar{x}_{c\cdot} + u_c + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

and the **within–between** formulation recommended by @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects enters the departure and the mean instead,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_W \left( x_{ct} - \bar{x}_{c\cdot} \right) + \beta_B\, \bar{x}_{c\cdot} + u_c + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

where $\beta_W$ is the slope within countries and $\beta_B$ the slope between countries. The two equations are one model in two parameterisations, with $\beta = \beta_W$ and $\pi = \beta_B - \beta_W$, and Bell and Jones prefer the second, among other reasons because "with temporal data it is more interpretable, as the within and between effects are clearly separated" (p. 142). The fits presented below use `lmer()` from lme4 [@BatesEtAl2015FittingLinearMixedeffects], the standard R package for mixed models, called through lmerTest [@KuznetsovaEtAl2017LmerTestPackageTests], a package that adds degrees of freedom to the tests. In these fits the random-intercept term `(1 | cntry)` corresponds to $u_c$, and `datawizard::demean()` returns the country mean of a variable and the departure of each row from it.

```{r}
#| label: rewb-fit
#| message: false
# the country mean of unemployment (unemp_between) and the departure of each
# year from it (unemp_within)
europeanisation_wb <- datawizard::demean(europeanisation, select = "unemp", by = "cntry")

m_mundlak <- lmerTest::lmer(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_between + (1 | cntry), data = europeanisation_wb)
m_wb <- lmerTest::lmer(mcosmo ~ unemp_within + unemp_between + (1 | cntry), data = europeanisation_wb)

summary(m_mundlak)$coefficients
summary(m_wb)$coefficients
```

```{r}
#| label: rewb-values
#| include: false
wb_coef <- summary(m_wb)$coefficients
mu_coef <- summary(m_mundlak)$coefficients
```

Read the slopes against everything fitted so far. The coefficient on unemployment in the Mundlak form and the within slope of the within–between form are the same number, `r insight::format_value(wb_coef["unemp_within", "Estimate"], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")`, which is *exactly* the estimate with country fixed effects from section 4 (`m_country`), because separating out the variation between countries is what fixed effects do. The between slope is `r insight::format_value(wb_coef["unemp_between", "Estimate"], digits = 4, style_positive = "plus")`, positive and imprecise, and the coefficient on the country mean in the Mundlak form, `r insight::format_value(mu_coef["unemp_between", "Estimate"], digits = 4, style_positive = "plus")`, is the difference between the two slopes. The puzzle posed by the pooled fit in section 3 now finds an arithmetic answer, since the pooled slope of `r insight::format_value(coef(m_lm)[["unemp"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` was a weighted blend of `r insight::format_value(wb_coef["unemp_within", "Estimate"], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` and `r insight::format_value(wb_coef["unemp_between", "Estimate"], digits = 4, style_positive = "plus")`, two patterns with opposite signs averaged into a figure close to zero. The Hausman test also rejects for the same reason, namely because $\beta_W \neq \beta_B$, and as @BellEtAl2019FixedRandomEffects [p. 1057] put it, the test, "[a]lthough often (mis)used as a test of whether FE or RE models 'should' be used ..., it is really a test of whether there is a contextual effect, or whether the between and within effects are different".

The test of $\pi$ in the Mundlak form is that same comparison, and it can be carried out with cluster-robust errors, just as the slope was tested in section 4. Since the coefficients of the Mundlak form are the same when the equation is fitted by pooled OLS, the difference can be tested under the CR2 rule of the workshop with errors clustered by country:

```{r}
#| label: rewb-cr2
#| message: false
m_mundlak_ols <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_between, data = europeanisation_wb)
mundlak_cr2 <- clubSandwich::coef_test(m_mundlak_ols, vcov = "CR2", cluster = europeanisation_wb$cntry,
                                       coefs = "unemp_between", test = "Satterthwaite")
mundlak_cr2
```

The difference between the two slopes is significant at the 5% level under the rule of the curve (`r insight::format_p(mundlak_cr2$p_Satt, stars = FALSE, digits = 3)` on `r insight::format_value(mundlak_cr2$df_Satt, digits = 1)` Satterthwaite degrees of freedom), as it is under the model-based errors of the within–between fit (`r insight::format_p(bwc$p_difference, stars = FALSE, digits = 3)`), and for the cosmopolitan share and unemployment the assumption of random effects thus fails under every test applied in the workshop. The same comparison also offers a first encounter with the estimand, the quantity that an analysis sets out to estimate. 'The effect of unemployment on EU framing' has a value within countries and a value between countries, and choosing a model means choosing which of the two you are asking for. In the view of Bell and Jones, this formulation should usually replace the contest between fixed and random effects.

The two associations are drawn in @fig-between-within, which sets the 27 country means of the cosmopolitan share against the 27 country means of unemployment, with the slope fitted across these means, beside the deviations of each country-year from the means of its own country, with the slope within countries drawn through the deviations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-between-within
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-cap: "The association between countries and within them, for the cosmopolitan share and unemployment. Left: the mean of each member state over 2004–2013, with the least-squares slope across the 27 means. Right: each country-year as a deviation from the means of its own country, with the slope within countries, which is the slope with country fixed effects and the within slope of the within–between model. Sources: `data/display_country_means.csv`, `data/display_between_within.csv` and the workshop panel."
#| code-fold: true
within_pts <- datawizard::demean(europeanisation, select = c("unemp", "mcosmo"), by = "cntry")
p_between <- ggplot2::ggplot(cmeans, ggplot2::aes(unemp_mean, mcosmo_mean)) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(intercept = mean(cmeans$mcosmo_mean) - bwc$b_between * mean(cmeans$unemp_mean),
                       slope = bwc$b_between, colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "grey45", size = 1.6) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = cntry), size = 2.6, colour = "grey30", nudge_y = 0.013) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Between countries", x = "mean unemployment, 2004–2013 (%)",
                y = "mean cosmopolitan share") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
p_within <- ggplot2::ggplot(within_pts, ggplot2::aes(unemp_within, mcosmo_within)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey85") +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey85") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "grey60", size = 1) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = bwc$b_within, colour = "#a10000", linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", format(x))) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", format(x))) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Within countries", x = "unemployment, deviation from the country mean (points)",
                y = "cosmopolitan share, deviation") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_between, p_within)
```

Across the countries the association is positive, at `r insight::format_value(bwc$b_between, digits = 4, style_positive = "plus")` per point of unemployment with `r insight::format_p(bwc$p_between, stars = FALSE, digits = 2)` on 25 degrees of freedom and a correlation of `r insight::format_value(bwc$r_between, digits = 2)` between the two sets of means, indicating that the countries with higher unemployment over the decade did not frame the EU in less cosmopolitan terms, and that the pattern, if anything, appears to run the other way. Within countries, by contrast, the association is negative, at `r insight::format_value(bwc$b_within, digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` with a CR2 p-value of `r insight::format_value(bwc$p_within_cr2, digits = 4)`. The model-based test of the difference rejects the equality of the two slopes for the positive composite as well (`r insight::format_p(bw$p_difference[bw$outcome == "mpos" & bw$predictor == "unemp"], stars = FALSE, digits = 3)`), while for the utilitarian scale the same test yields `r insight::format_p(bw$p_difference[bw$outcome == "mutil" & bw$predictor == "unemp"], stars = FALSE, digits = 3)`. For growth, both slopes of the cosmopolitan share are positive, the direction expected by the claim for growth, but only the slope across countries is clearly different from zero (`r insight::format_p(bwg$p_between, stars = FALSE, digits = 3)`, against a CR2 p of `r insight::format_value(bwg$p_within_cr2, digits = 2)` within countries).

These results settle where the options for the Estimator decision that do not hold the comparison within countries belong. Random effects is consistent only if the stable differences between countries are unrelated to the predictor, a condition rejected by the test of the two slopes, and pooled OLS is a blend of the same two associations, both estimators thus remaining off the curve of the claim. The within–between model would repeat points already contained in the curve, since its within slope equals the slope with country effects exactly, and its use lies in showing the two associations side by side, as the figure does. A reader who wishes to ask the cross-national question will find its answer in the regression on country means, outside the curve of the claim, while the reasons for each option are recorded on the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-estimand).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Add a dummy for each year to the pooled Mundlak regression, `lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_between + factor(year), data = europeanisation_wb)`, and check that the coefficient on `unemp` becomes the two-way slope of section 4 to the last digit, since the year dummies now remove the common European path as the year effects did. Then test the coefficient on `unemp_between` with `clubSandwich::coef_test()` as above, and say in one sentence what the test compares in the two-way design.
:::

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The models presented in this module are executed on the page from the committed workshop panel `europeanisation_cy.csv` and from the files of results written beside it by the case-study pipeline, whose CR2 test comes from the clubSandwich package in `R/_curve_tools.R`, while the [data codebook](../data/europeanisation_cy_codebook.md) documents the country-year construction and the definitions of the items.

The estimators are those implemented in the fixest and plm packages [@BergeEtAl2026FastUserfriendlyEconometrics; @CroissantMillo2023PanelDataEconometrics] and in lme4 [@BatesEtAl2015FittingLinearMixedeffects], and the econometric treatment of fixed effects, random effects, the Hausman test and the Mundlak device is given at length by @Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross. For the same material written for sociologists, @Allison2009FixedEffectsRegression offers a short introduction to fixed-effects regression and @Halaby2004PanelModelsSociological a review of panel models in sociological research. The Mundlak device goes back to @Mundlak1978PoolingTimeSeries and the specification test to @Hausman1978SpecificationTestsEconometrics, while @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects and @BellEtAl2019FixedRandomEffects make the case for the within–between model. On clustered errors and few clusters, @CameronMiller2015PractitionersGuideClusterrobust wrote the guide for practitioners, and the CR2 correction and its degrees of freedom derive from @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard, @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust and @ImbensKolesar2016RobustStandardErrors, with the wild cluster bootstrap presented in @MacKinnonWebb2017WildBootstrapInference. The data structure of comparative surveys repeated over time is discussed by @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling, and the problem of ecological inference was described by @Robinson1950EcologicalCorrelationsBehavior.
